newsitem.title: USA: Stg/mark to fall, deflate dlr, Irish punt-Goldman.
newsitem.headline: Stg/mark to fall, deflate dlr, Irish punt-Goldman.

text.p: The British pound now stands 18 percent over its equilibrium rate against the mark, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs & Co, who said its probable decline may also bring an end to the recent surge in dollar/mark and the Irish pound.

Meanwhile, the yen will continue to strengthen toward 108 to the dollar and 60 to the mark from current rates of 113 and 64, respectively, according to Goldman's Weekly Analyst, a trading report released to clients on Tuesday.
Goldman's model estimates sterling/mark should trade at 2.50 marks, or 2.65 when incorporating special factors, well below the current rate near 2.97.

"It is hard to find any technique which comes up with an estimate higher than 2.65 ... unless we make exceptionally friendly forecasts for the UK and pessimistic for Germany," according to the report, a copy of which Reuters obtained on Wednesday.
In addition, the vibrant pound will balloon Britain's current account deficit to above two percent of GDP in 1998 unless the pound falls, the report said.
Goldman recommended selling sterling and the dollar as it nears 1.77 marks.
Opportunities to sell dollar/mark may arise "from a setback in sterling/mark or more directly from a continued narrowing in the U.S.-German bond spread," the report stated.
The Irish pound, currently trading near 2.68 marks, could suffer if sterling/mark falls, though several fundamental factors currently support the punt, Goldman said.
"A large part of the current (punt/mark) is probably a spinoff of the overvalued sterling/mark rate," the report said. "If the pound drops, (punt/mark) strength is unlikely to persist."

A solid Irish trade surplus and estimated 1997 GDP growth of seven percent help explain the punt's vigor and could push the unit higher against sterling from its current rate near 90 pence, Goldman said.
"Our analysis does suggest that the Irish pound is quite cheap compared to sterling," the report stated.

The current punt/mark rate suggests the market believes the punt will be revalued by seven percent prior to proposed European Economic and Monetary Union, which would be a poor policy move if sterling declines, Goldman said.
"Ireland would not have the option to realign the punt once EMU begins, so they really need to think carefully about" its fair value, Goldman said.
Goldman recommended selling the Irish pound against the lira and Finnish markka.
